measured-scalar.description: The latest scalar emitted by a repeatable measurement source. Authored lf-num text freezes the value a version states; the source snapshot records whether that measurement ran again.

text-document.description: UTF-8 text from a file or a selected line range.

lf-ask.description: One complete Ask for the user: begin with one direct heading stating the question, so the Ask names itself without the page around it, then include any context or evidence needed to answer it and exactly one non-quoted widget whose declaration names a local Ask through x-awaits or x-request.ask. The nested widget still owns the action or external-request lifecycle and determines whether the Ask is open. The authored heading is the Ask's title: it stays in the document's reading, gives the Asks tray its name, and is where `a`/`A` arrives. Keep an ordinary semantic section around the Ask when the document needs a section landmark. The wrapper adds no frame or caption of its own.

lf-gloss.description: A short, plain-text explanation attached to a phrase: hover the phrase to glance at it, Tab to its Explain control to reach it by keyboard, or click or tap the phrase to keep it open; Escape and a click elsewhere close it. Use one for a local term, acronym, or premise whose meaning a user may want without leaving the sentence — not for a citation, a qualification the argument depends on, or an aside long enough to deserve visible prose, a details disclosure, or a sidenote. The phrase and `tip` are both the page's words: the phrase stays in its sentence, and the explanation can be selected, quoted, and commented on while open. A printout puts the explanation after the phrase as a quiet parenthetical note, so no authored meaning depends on hover or script; keep the phrase out of parentheses of your own, or the printout nests them. Keep the explanation self-contained and write it at the first useful occurrence rather than marking every repetition.
lf-gloss.x-example: Deploy through a <lf-gloss tip="A thin, end-to-end path through the real system.">walking skeleton</lf-gloss> before parallelizing.

lf-num.description: One measured scalar frozen into the sentence that states it. Write the displayed value, unit included, as the element text; bind `source` to the repeatable measurement feed and set `at` to the `updated` instant `leaf data set` printed for that snapshot; `authoring-evidence.md`, Measured facts, has the workflow and the staleness check. `via` may preserve the human-readable command or query in markup when the source id alone is not enough provenance. Use lf-metric instead when the number is a headline KPI in a metric row, and ordinary text for a number that is not produced by a repeatable measurement.
lf-num.x-example: The import now takes <lf-num source="import-latency" at="2026-08-27T09:00:00Z" via="uv run bench-import">184 ms</lf-num> at p95.

lf-text-document.description: A file-backed text document supplied through Leaf data. `source` binds the page-owned feed. `language` colors the document with one of $languages. `label` names the document above the exact text; without it the source id does. Lines longer than the column wrap, since a capture has no alignment to keep, and print wraps them too so nothing is cut off on paper. Put the widget inside ordinary details or an lf-tab when the document should begin collapsed or in a separate view.

lf-toc.description: A table of contents derived from the page's h2-h6 headings. `max-level` sets the deepest heading included when lower-level headings are local detail rather than page destinations; omitting it includes every level. A scrolling document with two or more included headings places one in an `aside.sidebar` near the opening by default; omit it when the outline is already visible at a glance. Root workspaces use their region navigation instead of a page-wide contents sidebar, and root page tabs supply their own view navigation. In the roomy margin, the runtime distributes the page title and headings down a full-height spine according to the sections they lead, paints the visible band of the document on that spine, and reveals every generated label on pointer or keyboard entry. Crowded destinations bend together on one fitted scale so every marker and label remains distinct; when the labels cannot physically fit, the widget becomes an ordinary open, scrollable outline. In flow and on paper, it remains an ordinary open outline. A heading that titles an identified section links to the section, keeping an eyebrow and heading together at arrival and giving the public fragment the section's id. Otherwise an existing heading id becomes the target; for an id-less heading, the widget adds a position-derived target beside it without changing the authored heading. Live links reveal headings inside disclosures or tabs, and a copied link returns to the same version's section. A stable authored section or heading id keeps that target across versions. The generated labels are link apparatus rather than a second commentable copy of each heading, and version diffs ignore them as generated navigation. Write the element empty and give it a stable id.

lf-activity.description: A feed of what has happened on the page, newest first, read from the event log. Each row names who moved (You for the user, the agent by its name, Page for a default the page applied), what they did, where, and how long ago: comments and reactions with their opening words, replies, resolutions and reopenings, widget actions worded from each verb's record form in the words of the version the user acted on or, for a verb that creates a child, from the child's words, reports, requests and their receipts, published versions with their changelog, and approvals. A gesture the user took back stays in place marked undone. Read receipts, deliveries, summaries, titles, and errors stay out. The place is the way there: a widget or section row is a fragment link, and a thread row opens that thread. It shows the latest 50 rows and stores nothing; the log is its only input. Place it when the user will come back to a page that several hands change over time (a working board, a hub, a long review) and needs to see what moved since they last looked; a page read once does not need one. Put it last in the column or in a pane of its own, write the element empty, and give it a stable id.

lf-options.description: The alternatives in a question the user answers. Put a live group inside lf-ask, where any premise or evidence shared by every alternative leads into the choices; the group itself contains only options and controls. Children are lf-option elements only. An option leading with a <strong> title becomes a full-width card; put its case and decision-relevant evidence or preview there instead of in separate alternative sections. Bare-label options render as compact rows for alternatives that need no case beyond the label. A row may use `for` only when the choice selects among sections or work items that already exist independently of the decision; do not create sections merely to hold the alternatives. With `choose` (which requires an id), the group draws as one control and takes the user's pick by click or keyboard. `multiple` (which requires `choose`) allows a set. It says whether two options can both hold, not whether the user usually picks one: without it a second pick replaces the first and the announcement names only the new pick, so nothing tells the user their first answer is gone. Leave it off only where the options rule each other out; where a set is answerable — work to start, checks to run, risks to accept — allow it. The marks say "choose one" or "choose any" to a screen reader; do not repeat that instruction in the question. On the page the last cell is an `Another option` field for an answer the author did not list. It takes the next Ask digit after the authored options when one of the nine addresses remains, or Tab reaches it; Shift+Enter writes a newline, and Enter adds the option on physical keyboards. On touch keyboards, Enter writes a newline and the Add control submits. Because that field takes any unlisted answer, author the alternatives you mean and no catch-all beside them: a `Something else` option takes a click where the field takes the answer. Adding sends an `add` action naming the new option's id and words, then selects it through the ordinary `choose` action; it does not start a thread. In a thread the thread's reply box already owns that role, and Enter from an option mark continues there. The pick reaches the agent as a `choose` action naming every picked option. A single-choice pick answers its Ask; a multiple-choice Ask stays open until the user presses Done, whose `answer` action states the set is complete on the page or in a thread. An added option stands on its own: a later pick leaves it in the group, undoing the `add` removes it, and it remains effective across revisions. To ask what one means, open a thread on it with `leaf thread open <page> --section <option-id>`; to incorporate one, write it as an ordinary lf-option with the same id and words. An authored `chosen` pick still leaves a multiple-choice Ask waiting for the user's Done. `settled` (also requiring an id) collapses a retired decision to a disclosure naming the chosen option while preserving every option and anchor.

Where should run status appear?

Both choices preserve the existing run detail.

effort: lowrisk: medrecommended Status on the run list One join; failures are visible without a click. effort: nonerisk: low Leave the list alone No work; failures stay one click away.

lf-option.description: One alternative in a decision. Direct prose text uses inline Markdown, so block syntax such as lists, headings, and fenced code does not render; element children remain HTML. Default to a <strong> title and one sentence naming the consequence. When comparison facts help, show the same two or three chips across its siblings. Keep decision-relevant evidence or a preview inside the option, but add a fact rail, paragraphs, or a nested visual only when the choice cannot be made from that compact face. A short label alone renders as a compact row for an alternative that needs no case beyond the label. `for` may point that row at an existing section or work item only when the target remains useful independently of this decision; it never supplies the row's words. `chosen` records the user's pick in authored state; a final `recommended` chip is only advice (see lf-chip). Rewriting a picked option needs `restated`, and `$restated` in `registry.json` says when to rewrite one rather than correct it beside the Ask; the other options may change freely.

lf-chip.description: One short label in the band above an option's or a variant's title. Comparison chips name what the alternatives differ on, in the words that fit them. `effort: low` and `risk: high` are worth starting from, since most decisions do turn on those two, but they are a suggestion and nothing more — `blast-radius: high`, `backward compat: no`, `cost: £240`, `migration: two tables` are the same slot, and a chip is as free in its answer as in its name: a scale of your own, a yes or a no, a quantity, a few words. Write comparison chips before the <strong> title (a lf-variant takes them the same way, being the same shape without the decision), and write the same ones on every option in the group, in the same order, so they read down it. An ordinary final chip such as `<lf-chip tone="ok">recommended</lf-chip>` may mark the author's preferred option, while the reason stays in the option's prose. It is advice, while `chosen` alone records the user's pick. Chips are the glance and not the comparison — two or three an eye takes in before it reads, where a `<dl class="facts">` rail is the dimensions the options are argued on at whatever length that takes. An option can carry both, and only the rail costs a card its terseness: a `<dl>` is block content, so it stacks the group into rows, and chips never do. `tone` tints a chip — the layer's own vocabulary, `$tones.names`, which the author can query in `registry.json` — and is the author's judgement about this answer, not a property of the facet: `risk: high` is red because you say so, and the same word on another page may not be. Leave it off and the chip is neutral, which is what most of them should be; colour that lands on every chip has stopped pointing at anything. It is the same bargain `lf-metric` makes with `direction` — the theme knows the tints, the author knows which way is good.

lf-milestones.description: A milestone schedule with status markers on a rail. Its members are lf-milestone elements only.
lf-milestones.x-example: Survey the sites Map sun and squirrel routes. Build the feeders Two classic, two heated. Install and watch

lf-milestone.description: One milestone. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. `status` colors the rail marker; `when` is a free-text schedule label; `tags` is a comma-separated list rendered as chips.

lf-chronology.description: A chronology of what happened and when — the incident-report shape. Its members are lf-chronology-entry elements only. Where lf-milestones tracks planned work by status, lf-chronology records observed facts and interventions.
lf-chronology.x-example: Feeder camera offline Battery alert from the north feeder. Battery swapped Camera back Feed resumed.

lf-chronology-entry.description: One entry in a chronology. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. `at` is a free-text time label; `kind` colors the rail marker.

lf-compare.description: Labeled variants — neutral exhibition, where lf-options is a decision. Children are lf-variant elements only. Layout follows lf-options: terse variants sit side by side, block content in any variant stacks the group into rows, and a `<dl class="facts">` after the label docks as an aligned rail.
lf-compare.x-example: Cedar Weathers silver; no sealant. Pine Cheaper; seal it yearly.

lf-variant.description: One variant in a comparison. Lead with a <strong> label; any content follows, widgets included.

lf-metric.description: One headline number as a tile: element text is the label, `value` the headline number, `delta` a signed change (leading + or -), `direction` says which sign is good (up-good, up-bad) so the delta colors honestly; without it the delta stays neutral. A row of metrics is an lf-grid of lf-metric tiles.
lf-metric.x-example:
<lf-grid id="k-row">
  <lf-metric id="k-visits" value="312" delta="+41" direction="up-good">daily visits</lf-metric>
  <lf-metric id="k-refills" value="2.1/wk" delta="+0.4" direction="up-bad">refills</lf-metric>
  <lf-metric id="k-species" value="14">species seen</lf-metric>
</lf-grid>

lf-tree.description: A file tree from an indent-notation body: one node per line, children indented deeper, a trailing / marking a directory, trailing +N/-N tokens rendering as change badges. Body is data — text inside its <pre>, HTML-escaped (& first, then < and >).
lf-tree.x-example:
feeders/
  mount.py  +2 -2
  schedule.py  +1
  sites/
    north.toml

lf-code.description: An annotated code block — the walkthrough shape. The body is the code verbatim inside its <pre> (data, HTML-escaped — & first, then < and > — column 0); `language` colors it, naming one of $languages; `hi` highlights line ranges ("3-5,8"); lf-note children sit beside that <pre> and anchor remarks at lines by number. For an excerpt of a longer file, `lines` gives the source line numbers the body quotes, in that range grammar and ascending ("1505-1507,1520-1527" is a 3-line and an 8-line stretch): the gutter shows those numbers, each gap between ranges draws an elided row, and `hi` and a note's `at` name lines by those numbers too. A number in a gap addresses its elided row: a note whose `at` falls there captions it, saying what was left out. Without `lines` the body is lines 1 to N. Leave `language` off where the body isn't source (a transcript, command output) — nothing guesses, so an undeclared block stays plain.
lf-code.x-example:
def bracket(temp):
    if temp < 0:
        return "steel"
    return "cedar"
Freezing is the only threshold that matters.

lf-note.description: A remark anchored at a line of its lf-code parent. Prose content; `at` is the line's number as the block numbers it — 1-based, or from the block's `lines`. A line an excerpt leaves out docks the note on the elided row standing for it, as that row's caption.

lf-chart.description: A chart drawn from a comma-separated body: the header row names the x column and then one column per series, and every row after it is one x value and its numbers (blank where a series has none). The body is data, not prose: text inside its <pre>, HTML-escaped (& first, then the angle brackets). `kind` says which picture — bars (a group of bars per x value), rows (horizontal bars, for long names or a ranking), stack (bars stacked into a total, so no negatives), line (a run over time or an ordered x), dots (two numbers against each other, x column numeric). `y` names what the numbers are. A bar's x is one slot per row whatever it says; a line or a scatter reads its column, so dates (2026-06-01, or 2026-06 for a month) get a time axis and numbers a numeric one. Two rows may not share an x value, and a series column may not be empty. At most $series.steps series — fold the small ones together or split the chart. There is no pie, because the comparison it asks for is between angles and the comparison bars ask for is between lengths. Comments anchor to the required id, not to text inside the drawing.

week, backend, frontend
2026-05-04, 31, 18
2026-05-11, 26, 21
2026-05-18, 19, 14
2026-05-25, 12, 11

lf-shot.description: A before/after pair of screenshots under one draggable divider. Drag the divider or use its Arrow, Home, and End keys; click the image to switch endpoints, choose Before or After from the rail above it, or use the target’s round margin entry. The margin entry’s split circle fills the left half for before and the right half for after, and its hover label names the next endpoint. `before` and `after` are served image paths that `leaf page media` prints (see `authoring-evidence.md`, Source files and media). `alt` says what the pair shows, for a user who can't see it. The element takes no content: what the page has to say about the change is ordinary prose written around it, where the user can quote it. Where the change is what a decision turns on, the pair goes inside the lf-option proposing it, so the user compares it and presses in one place. Reach for it when the change reads at page scale — layout, spacing, a component swapped out. Below that scale the column's width is against you: crop the pair to the part that moved, or show the element itself before and after at real size.

lf-board.description: A kanban board the user edits directly: cards move between columns or reorder within one — dragged by the grip, moved with direct column buttons on phones, or moved by keyboard (the grip is a button: Enter grabs, arrows move, Enter drops) — and each completed move reaches the agent as a `move` action naming the card, target column, and the card's rank there. Children are lf-column elements only. A version that changes a moved card's column writes the card where the move put it, and later versions keep it there unless they mark it `restated` (`authoring-revisions.md`, Honor user state); the restatement gate refuses one that moves it silently. The user-origin reading and version diff compare a card's column only: a reorder within one column is not called out as a separate state change. A move rests on its card, so a rewrite retracts it through the card (see lf-card), never the board.
lf-board.x-example: Heated perch Wire the south feeder. Squirrel baffle Camera mount

lf-column.description: One column on a board. `label` is the column heading, and the name a screen reader announces for the list of cards beneath it — so it has to read as the column's name on its own. Children are lf-card elements only; an empty column is a valid drop target. `tone` marks what landing in the column means (danger for a column that blocks, warn for one that needs a look, ok for done); a dot before the column's heading carries it, so leave it off a column whose name says nothing about status. The heading row also shows how many cards the column holds.

lf-card.description: One card on a board. Lead with a <strong> title; prose follows. The user drags it by its grip; the id names it in `move` actions and keeps comment anchors stable across moves. Rewriting a card the user has moved needs `restated` on the card (see `$restated` in `registry.json`).

lf-tabs.description: A tab set presenting several views of one page. When it is the final substantive child of main and the only substantive content before it is one native header or nothing, the set becomes borderless page navigation and each tab owns the content area; use this for project-scale views that share one history, Threads panel, Ask inventory, and revision sequence. Any other placement leaves it a framed tabbed section for local alternatives within surrounding content. Put the shared title and lede inside the optional header before a root set, put the primary current view first, and remove an earlier view once the current work no longer depends on it, keeping the context it still needs, and any passage whose id anchors an open thread or holds a standing decision, in a collapsed details inside the relevant tab. Ordering gives the first panel emphasis and makes it the default for a user with no remembered panel or reading position. A saved panel or restored position takes precedence because the open tab is the user's display state — remembered per browser tab like scroll position, never an action, never carried by a version. Each lf-tab is a self-contained view with its own prose and widgets, while Threads, Asks, versions, and sign-off remain global. Links, find-in-page, Ask travel, comment-anchor jumps, and reading-position restore open the owning tab. Switching page tabs puts the panel's id in the URL, so Back and Forward return to earlier views and a fragment naming content inside a panel opens that panel; a switch leaves the strip where it is on screen and reopens each view where the user last read it. Its members are lf-tab elements only; unupgraded, panels stack as labeled sections.
lf-tabs.x-example:

Keep the original outcome and constraints in reach.

lf-tab.description: One view in a tab set. `label` names its tab in the strip (and the stacked heading before upgrade). In page navigation, its content is an ordinary document view or one workspace; page tabs in the same set may mix those forms. In a tabbed section, prose, sections, and widgets nest freely. Ids inside share the page's one universe, so keep them distinct across tabs.

lf-draft.description: A block of text the user owns: they press it (or its ✎ button) to rewrite it in place, and the exact words reach the agent as an `edit` action naming the element. After the first edit, Changes shows a bounded, lossless word-aligned difference from this version, every recorded body in order, and a Restore control for each older body; very large divergent middles appear as one replacement rather than freezing the page. Restoring posts another ordinary `edit`, so it converges across tabs and later versions instead of creating private undo state. The body is the draft text verbatim inside its <pre> (data, HTML-escaped — & first, then < and >; newlines preserved). It carries no Ask chrome of its own — put a draft inside a lf-card where the column is the verdict, or let page sign-off approve the page as a whole. Usable anywhere prose flows. The agent rewriting prose of its own goes in a lf-suggestion instead; a draft is the user's own words, so there is nothing for them to accept. Once they have edited one those words are theirs: re-emit the body you wrote and their edit still stands over it — and `leaf thread open` reads it their way, quoting the words their edit left and refusing the ones it replaced. To take the pen back — a fact of yours to fix in a sentence they rewrote — write the new text and mark the element `restated` (see `$restated` in `registry.json`).
lf-draft.x-example: Adds --dry-run to every mutating command.

lf-specimen.description: A specimen of page content. Ordinary children render as static quotation: a muted gutter and a small-caps quoted label, with widget actions disabled. For an operable complete Leaf page, put its main content in one direct template[data-specimen] with a stable id. The optional label names the specimen and its frame. Keep invented content visibly fictional. See page-authoring.md, Live specimens, for child-page authoring, interaction, reset, and isolation.
lf-specimen.x-example: effort: lowPaper maps Nothing to charge. effort: medDedicated GPS Offline maps, week-long battery. My take: this is the better field tool.

lf-grid.description: Places blocks in two dimensions. In a column page it takes the column's width, as a paragraph does, so its tiles line up with the prose; `data-width="wide"` or `data-width="available"` asks for more, as on a figure, for a board or surfaces that need room past the prose. On a wide page (`<main data-width="available">`) it takes the page's width. Each direct child is one cell, and each cell is a frame: what it holds takes the cell's width, text keeps the reading measure, and a surface fills the cell. Without `columns` the grid fits as many equal columns as the width allows; `columns` takes a count (at most that many equal columns, fewer when the width runs out) or a template of fr tracks such as `1fr 2fr`, which stacks into one column where its narrowest track would be narrower than 14rem, the least a counted column takes (a `2fr 1fr` grid below 43.5rem, a `3fr 2fr` grid below 36.5rem), and stacks on paper. Cells keep authored order and align to their top. Nest a grid in a cell for a cell that spans rows. Let the grid place its cells: page CSS that sets a grid's own `display`, `grid-*`, or `position` fights it, and `version check` says so.

lf-workspace.description: Task regions kept together while the space allows. It takes all the room the page shell leaves. As `main`'s only block, with the page title in its optional direct header, or as a page tab's only block, it also takes the window's height: when that height and width hold it, each pane's body scrolls on its own and the header and footer stay in view; when they don't, the panes take their natural height and the page scrolls, with the grid keeping the columns its width allows. Anywhere else it is embedded and stays in document flow. Its direct header and footer frame exactly one body element: an lf-grid of lf-pane regions, one lf-pane, or a widget that arranges its own regions, such as a playground, alone or in an Ask of a heading and that widget. Only those take the height, so a plain div or section around one leaves it flowing. A narrow window stacks the regions in authored order, so choose an order that still reads stacked; a standalone copy keeps the workspace's columns at the copy's width and lets the page scroll.

lf-pane.description: One reading region in a workspace: an optional direct header, exactly one body element, and an optional direct footer. Its label names the region accessibly; the header supplies any visible heading. While its workspace holds the window the body scrolls on its own under the header and above the footer; otherwise the pane is an ordinary section and the page scrolls. Wrap several blocks in one div or section to make the body. Put action widgets in its direct footer when they should stay reachable while the body scrolls.
